title: Is your AI receptionist working? 5 Signs to check monthly
summary: Most businesses turn on an AI receptionist and never check what it did. Here are the 5 signs to tell you if it's deflecting or losing calls.
body_markdown:
Your goal in setting up an AI receptionist was to stop missing calls. A few months in, and you can’t say for sure whether it’s doing that or whether callers reach it and hang up.


Many businesses monitor an[AI receptionist](https://www.quo.com/product/ai/receptionist) closely for the first couple of weeks, then stop. They assume it’s working. But an AI receptionist might have problems that go unnoticed. It might be helpful to some callers and frustrating to others. Without digging deeper, both calls appear to be handled.


Without checking to see what happens after the call, you may not realize your customers are annoyed or that you’ve lost business.


So is your AI receptionist working? Several signs can tell you that. We’ve rounded up five clear indicators, plus where to find them and what they tell you.


##


**5 Signs to look at to tell if your AI receptionist is working**


To answer the question “Is my AI receptionist working?” you can pull a few numbers and sample calls from your call logs. Each of the five signs below tells you something different.


Sign What it tells you When it’s a red flag


Number of calls the AI receptionist answers compared to the total number of calls How much of your call volume does the AI receptionist take on? The count stays flat or drops after launch. It might mean calls aren’t reaching the AI receptionist.


Calls resolved without a human Whether callers get the information they were looking for. For example, they called to ask about your hours and got an answer. You look at a sample of calls, and the caller’s needs aren’t being met by the AI receptionist.


Calls transferred to a person Whether the right calls reach your team You don’t want to see callers asking for a human and not being transferred or simple calls handed off that the AI receptionist should have handled.


Caller hang-ups on the AI receptionist Whether callers want a person or find the AI receptionist frustrating You don’t want to see the numbers going up over time, or that there are problems around certain call topics.


What questions callers ask the AI receptionist Whether it’s handling the right calls It can be a red flag if most calls are about things the AI receptionist wasn’t designed to handle.


Right now, there are no industry benchmarks for optimal AI receptionist performance. The most accurate results will come from comparing your own numbers from before your AI receptionist launch with after.


If you use a business phone system like Quo, you can find that information easily.


Quo[Analytics](https://www.quo.com/product/analytics) has data going back to the day you created your workspace, so you have a before-launch baseline. Quo also reports AI-handled calls separately from your team’s calls. So if you use[Sona](https://www.quo.com/sona) , Quo’s AI receptionist, that data won’t mix with your reps’ data.


The numbers might not be directly comparable, since the AI could be handling calls that were previously missed. But you could compare how many people hang up when they reach your voicemail with how many people hang up on the AI receptionist, for example. Over time, you can create month-over-month or quarter-over-quarter comparisons with your AI receptionist.


##


**Where to find each of the five signs**


You can find some signs, like calls answered, in your[call analytics](https://www.quo.com/blog/call-analytics/) . Others, like calls resolved without a human, require sampling call summaries or call transcripts to see what happened.


Signal Where to find it in Quo


Number of calls the AI answers Analytics or your call log


Calls resolved without a human Summaries and transcripts from a call sample


Calls transferred to a person Summaries and transcripts or AI call tags


Caller hangs up on the AI Analytics


Topics your callers ask AI Summaries and transcripts, or AI call tags


### **1. Number of calls the AI answers**


Open your call analytics dashboard and look under Incoming call outcomes. The Answered by agent count shows how many calls Sona picked up.


Compare this count against the total number of calls Answered by user in the period before launch. That tells you how many calls your agent is now handling. In the charts, you can see the percentage change from the prior period, such as the prior month, and a dashed comparison line on the chart itself.


If you use Quo as your business phone platform, Quo Analytics is available on the Business and Scale plans.


On the Starter plan, open your[call views](https://support.quo.com/core-concepts/inboxes/call-views) and filter for Handled by Sona. Use the date filter to look at all calls within a specific period of time.


If Sona answers more than one phone number for your business, run this check for each number.


### **2. Calls resolved without a human**


A resolved call is one where Sona handled the call from start to finish. Here’s what that looks like:


- **The caller got an answer** . Someone asked about your Saturday hours and got them. Or a caller asked whether you serve their ZIP code, and Sona confirmed that you do.
- **Sona captured everything your team needs to act.** A caller wants a quote for a kitchen remodel. Sona collects their contact details so your team can follow up and lets the caller know you’ll return the call later the same day.


To see how Sona is resolving calls, open your call views in Quo. Sample a set of around 20 Sona-handled calls and read each call summary. See whether the caller got the information they were looking for. If the summary isn’t clear, open the full transcript.


Repeat callers are another thing to check. Open the contact’s conversation history to see whether the same number called back within a day or two with the same issue or a follow-up. This might mean they didn’t get everything they needed.


### **3. Calls transferred to a person**


You can find calls Sona transferred to a human in two ways:


1. **Scan summaries and transcripts.** Filter your call views to Handled by Sona, then scan the summaries or transcripts for handoffs.
2. **Use AI call tags.** On the Scale plan, you can define a custom tag like “Caller asked for a person” or “Transfer needed” to help you narrow the calls faster.


Whether a transfer count is good or bad depends on what you set your AI receptionist up to do, like whether you set it up to answer common questions or mainly to route calls to the right place.


#### **Example: FAQs handled by Sona**


✅ If Sona mainly answers FAQs, a low transfer rate is a good sign that it’s handling the simple calls.


❌ A high rate means it’s missing questions it should be able to answer.


#### **Example: Transferred calls to a person**


✅ If Sona triages calls and routes callers to the right person, a high transfer rate means it’s working as designed.


❌ A low call transfer rate could mean callers gave up before reaching someone. It could also mean Sona is answering calls it should route.


### **4. Calls where the caller hangs up on the AI**


Open your Analytics and look under Incoming call outcomes for Agent Abandoned. This counts calls that reached an[AI voice agent](https://www.quo.com/product/ai/voice-agent) where the caller hung up in under 10 seconds.


Hang-ups can tell you a couple of things:


- The caller was turned off by an AI receptionist
- The caller wanted to speak to a human, and the greeting was too long or unclear


Track your call abandonment rate from month to month.


### **5. Topics your callers ask AI**


What callers ask about tells you whether Sona is handling the right calls. If a lot of calls cover topics it wasn’t set up for, it’s answering calls it shouldn’t. The same goes for calls that Sona attempts to handle that need a person from the start. Sona might also interact with spam and vendor pitches that it shouldn’t handle.


To find out, filter your call views to Handled by Sona. Sample 15 to 20 recent calls and note what each caller wanted. Then group the calls by topics, like booking, pricing questions, or complaints.


On the Scale plan, AI call tags can group calls by topic in your dashboard. Click any row to open that conversation and jump straight to the call.


##


**Warning signs your AI receptionist needs fixing**


You can set up your AI receptionist in many ways, depending on your business and the types of calls you want it to handle. If you see any of these warning signs, you may want to tweak your settings for better performance:


1. **Hang-ups are on the rise.** Callers are rejecting the AI by hanging up right after it answers. Check whether it’s one call type, like returning customers or after-hours calls, since a cluster points to a specific group the AI isn’t serving well. Then check whether the automated greeting from the AI receptionist makes it clear callers can reach a person.
2. **Callers’ needs aren’t met in the sample.** Sona picks up but doesn’t fully handle the call. Identify the unanswered questions and add that information to what Sona knows. Or instruct Sona to route those calls straight to your team.


1. **Volume stays flat after launch.** If Sona runs out of credits, it stops answering, and calls go to your call flow’s fallback path. Check your credit tier and either allow overages or move up a tier. You can also enable auto-charge to prevent disruption. Your setup can also be the cause. Sona may not be live on the number customers dial, or its call flow may be inactive. Open that number’s call flow and confirm the Sona step is published and the flow is active. Then check that the number matches the one on your website and ads.


1. **Spam and robocalls are included in the call count.** Robocalls can make up a large share of Sona’s calls. When that happens, the answered count rises, but calls from real customers stay flat or drop. In your sample, these show up as calls with no actual caller or customer request. Add a phone menu in front of Sona. Robocalls typically can’t respond to menu options, so most disconnect before reaching Sona.


##


**How to scale up your call review without listening to every call**


While a 20-call sample provides a pretty good overview of what’s going on, reading each call summary or transcript still takes time. You might also miss[conversation analytic](https://www.quo.com/blog/conversation-analytics/) trends across the hundreds of calls your AI handles in a month.


An AI assistant can help. Connect Quo to[Claude](https://www.quo.com/integrations/claude) ,[ChatGPT](https://www.quo.com/integrations/chatgpt) , or[Grok Bot](https://www.quo.com/integrations/grok-bot) through the Quo[MCP](https://www.quo.com/product/ai/mcp) . Then ask about your calls in plain language. For example:


*“Look at the calls Sona handled on \[phone number\] between \[start date\] and \[end date\]. For each call, tell me whether the caller got what they called for. List the calls where they didn’t, what the caller asked, and where Sona got stuck.”*


*“Look at the calls Sona handled on \[phone number\] between \[start date\] and \[end date\]. Group them by what the caller wanted and tell me how many calls fall into each group. Sona is set up to \[what Sona does, for example, book appointments and answer questions about hours and pricing\]. List any group that falls outside that, with an example of what a caller asked.”*


Quo users find that the MCP gives them more insights into their call data. Justin M., an independent consultant, calls Sona “a fantastic lightweight virtual receptionist” in a[G2 review](https://www.g2.com/products/quo-quo/reviews/quo-review-12695763) . He also says Quo’s API support makes it “easy for AI agents to connect via MCP.”


In addition to reviewing calls, the[Call log](https://www.quo.com/skills/call-log) and[Daily report](https://www.quo.com/skills/daily-report-template) skills can surface calls that need follow-up. Run these prompts every month so you can spot bigger trends.


##


**Give your AI receptionist a monthly checkup**


Your AI receptionist isn’t a one-time setup. What customers ask about changes over time, so plan to tweak how your voice agent handles those calls.


In Quo, Analytics shows how many calls Sona answered and how many callers hung up. Call summaries and transcripts show whether those calls went well. Once you connect an AI assistant through MCP, you can easily review calls in bulk.


Start by pulling this month’s numbers. They become your baseline. Then block off time on your calendar each month to do a review and comparison. That way, you won’t have to wonder, “Is my AI receptionist working?”

##


**FAQs**


****What percentage of calls should an AI receptionist handle on its own?****


There’s no benchmark, and anyone quoting a number is guessing. It depends on what you want your AI receptionist to do. It also depends on when it takes calls, like after hours or only when your team is busy. The more useful question is whether that number is changing. A resolved-without-a-human rate that falls month over month is a warning. It usually means callers are asking about things your AI receptionist isn’t set up to handle.


****How do you know if callers are hanging up on your AI receptionist?****


Look at the shortest AI-handled calls. In Quo, a call counts as answered by the AI agent once it reaches 10 seconds of talk time. Quo records anything shorter as Agent Abandoned. A rising count is a warning sign that callers hang up almost immediately.


****Is AI receptionist performance the same as voice agent analytics?****


While the two phrases are similar, they come from different places. AI voice agent analytics usually refers to tools developers use to monitor bots they built. Those tools track things like latency and model behavior. AI receptionist performance refers to the tool or feature in your business phone system and how well it handles calls. Measuring AI receptionist performance is part of your call reporting.
